9: The I2C IP is a controller-target combo that can function as an I<sup>2</sup>C controller and/or an I<sup>2</sup>C target.
10: These functional modules are enabled at runtime by setting the register fields [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) and [`CTRL.ENABLETARGET`](registers.md#ctrl).
11: If the Controller Module is to be used in a multi-controller environment, [`CTRL.MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN`](registers.md#ctrl) would also need to be set.
12: Note the ordering requirements in the register description for multi-controller configurations.
13: 
14: The SCL and SDA outputs from the block combine the SCL and SDA outputs from the Controller Module and Target Module.
15: The modules operate as though they were independent devices on the same I<sup>2</sup>C bus, with any logic low value taking priority.
16: 
17: On the input path, the IP's clock samples SCL and SDA after a 2-flop synchronizer.
18: However, the IP's input pins do not reflect the start point for the full input path delay, since pads and nets from I/O buffers also contribute.
19: The RTL parameter `InputDelayCycles` must be set to the maximum number of cycles of delay from the IP's output pin driving SCL or SDA to the IP's corresponding input pin sensing the transition.
20: `InputDelayCycles` can exclude the rise time that would be captured by [`TIMING1.T_R`](registers.md#timing1).
21: The reference point for `InputDelayCycles` is the clock edge after the launch clock edge.
22: In other words, a value of 0 means that the IP's 2-flop synchronizer would sample the IP's own outputs within one clock cycle (if the external pad driver could switch instantaneously).
23: 
24: ### Bus Monitor
25: 
26: The Bus Monitor block examines the SCL and SDA inputs and any transmitted outputs from the Controller Module and Target Module.
27: It detects START and STOP conditions and forwards the events.
28: In addition, it tracks whether a bus transaction is currently active and informs the Controller Module when the bus is free for it to transmit a new transaction.
29: Finally, it detects when bus arbitration is lost and informs the modules when they must release the bus and allow other devices to communicate.
30: 
31: For signaling when the bus is free, the behavior depends on whether [`CTRL.MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN`](registers.md#ctrl) is enabled.
32: If it's not enabled, the monitor merely observes the bus free time between transactions.
33: 
34: If multi-controller monitor mode is enabled, then the monitor also tracks transactions from other controllers, and it will report that the bus is busy until the free time expires after an external controller issues a STOP condition.
35: The bus can also become free after the [`HOST_TIMEOUT_CTRL`](registers.md#host_timeout_ctrl) duration expires, if the bus was left in the idle state, or it can become free in the case of a bus timeout (if enabled in [`TIMEOUT_CTRL`](registers.md#timeout_ctrl)).
36: 
37: At initial attachment in a multi-controller environment, typically the controller needs to wait until it determines the bus is free, and the initial state should be assumed to be busy.
38: To make this happen, [`HOST_TIMEOUT_CTRL`](registers.md#host_timeout_ctrl) should be programmed before enabling the bus monitor in [`CTRL`](registers.md#ctrl), and [`CTRL.MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN`](registers.md#ctrl) should be set either before or at the same time as enabling the Controller Module with [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl).
39: 
40: ### Controller Module
41: 
42: The Controller Module implements all mandatory controller features of the I<sup>2</sup>C protocol for multi-controller configurations, including clock synchronization and bus arbitration.
43: It also implements support for handling clock stretching.
44: 
45: The state-machine-controlled Controller Module allows for higher-speed operation with less frequent software interaction.
46: In this module, the I2C pins are controlled by the state machine, which in turn is controlled by a sequence of formatting indicators.
47: These indicators determine:
48: 
49: - The sequence of bytes which should be transmitted on the SDA and SCL pins.
50: - The periods between transmitted bytes when the state-machine should stop transmission and instead read back a fixed number of bytes.
51: - Which bytes should be preceded by a START symbol.
52: - Which bytes should be followed by a STOP symbol.
53: 
54: The format indicator consists of 13-bits.
55: That is of one single format byte (entered into the format FIFO through [`FDATA.FBYTE`](registers.md#fdata)), and five 1-bit flags (entered into the format FIFO through registers [`FDATA.READB`](registers.md#fdata), [`FDATA.RCONT`](registers.md#fdata), [`FDATA.START`](registers.md#fdata), [`FDATA.STOP`](registers.md#fdata) and [`FDATA.NAKOK`](registers.md#fdata))
56: 
57: The I2C Control Module reads each format indicator from the head of FMT_FIFO and processes them in turn.
58: If none of the flags are set for the format indicator, the I2C FSM simply transmits the format byte onto the SCL and SDA pins according to the specification, waits for acknowledgement, and then proceeds to the next format indicator.
59: The format flags modulate the behavior as follows:
60: 
61: - READB (corresponds to [`FDATA.READB`](registers.md#fdata)):
62: Signifies the format byte ([`FDATA.FBYTE`](registers.md#fdata)) should be treated as an unsigned number, R, and prompts the state machine to read R bytes from the target device.
63: Bytes read from the bus are inserted into the RX FIFO where they can be accessed by software.
64: A value of 0 is treated as a read of 256 bytes.
65: To read a larger byte stream, multiple 256-byte reads can be chained together using the RCONT flag.
66: - RCONT (corresponds to FIFO inputs [`FDATA.RCONT`](registers.md#fdata), only used with READB):
67:     - If RCONT is set, the format byte represents part of a longer sequence of reads, allowing for reads to be chained indefinitely.
68:     - The RCONT flag indicates the final byte returned with the current read should be responded to with an ACK, allowing the target to continue sending data.
69:     (Note that the first R-1 bytes read will still be acknowledged regardless of whether RCONT is asserted or not.)
70: - START (corresponds to [`FDATA.START`](registers.md#fdata), Ignored when used with READB):
71: Issue a START condition before transmitting the format byte on the bus.
72: This flag may also be used to issue a repeated start condition.
73: - STOP (corresponds to [`FDATA.STOP`](registers.md#fdata)):
74: Issue a STOP signal after processing this current entry in the FMT FIFO.
75: Note that this flag is not compatible with (READB & RCONT), and will cause bus conflicts.
76: - NAKOK (corresponds to [`FDATA.NAKOK`](registers.md#fdata), Not compatible with READB):
77: Typically every byte transmitted must also receive an ACK signal, and the IP will raise an exception if no ACK is received.
78: However, there are some I<sup>2</sup>C commands which do not require an ACK.
79: In those cases this flag should be asserted with FBYTE indicating no ACK is expected and no interrupt should be raised if the ACK is not received.
80: 
81: The Controller Module may proceed through all commands in the FMT FIFO as long as no exceptional event occurs.
82: If the Controller Module receives an unexpected NACK, a bus timeout occurs, or arbitration is lost while the Controller Module is transmitting, the module halts.
83: The module will not continue processing commands without software intervention.
84: 
85: Note that a full RX FIFO does not stop command processing.
86: Ensure the RX FIFO has enough space, else overflows can occur.
87: 
88: #### Controller NACK Handling
89: 
90: If the Controller Module transmits a byte and the 9th bit is a NACK from the Target/Bus, the `controller_halt` interrupt is usually asserted (modulo the effect of [`FDATA.NAKOK`](registers.md#fdata)).
91: If the `controller_halt` interrupt is asserted, the Controller FSM will halt until the interrupt condition has been cleared in the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.NACK`](registers.md#controller_events) register.
92: Software will likely want to do one of two things in handling this irq:
93: 1. End the current transaction by setting [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) to `1'b0`, and clear the FIFOs to be ready to begin a new transaction.
94: 2. Clear the FIFOs, then begin a new transfer without ending the transaction by adding new FDATA indicators to the FMTFIFO.
95:    In this case, the first entry written to the FMTFIFO should have [`FDATA.START`](registers.md#fdata) set to `1'b1` to create a repeated start condition.
96: 
97: Software should then clear the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.NACK`](registers.md#controller_events) to proceed with the next operation.
98: The `controller_halt` interrupt is a CIP status type, so it doesn't clear by writing to the [`INTR_STATE.CONTROLLER_HALT`](registers.md#intr_state) bit.
99: Instead, the `CONTROLLER_EVENTS` CSR tracks the contributing events, and all must be cleared for the interrupt to de-assert.
100: 
101: The Halt-on-NACK behaviour may be problematic if SW is not responsive, so there is a timeout mechanism that can automatically end the transaction by creating a STOP condition and returning to halt in an idle state.
102: This is configured using the [`HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT`](registers.md#host_nack_handler_timeout) CSR, which allows software to configure the delay before hardware will terminate the transaction.
103: When the timeout occurs, the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.UNHANDLED_NACK_TIMEOUT`] bit will set, and this condition will also cause the `controller_halt` interrupt to assert (or remain asserted).
104: Like the original NACK event, the timeout bit will cause the Controller Module to remain halted until it is cleared.
105: To continue with a new transaction, software should ensure that the `controller_halt` interrupt has been handled, with all contributing event bits cleared.
106: 
107: When the FSM first halts due to an unexpected NACK, there is still an ongoing transaction.
108: The Controller Module stops immediately following the (N)ACK bit's hold time after the SCL falling edge, and SCL remains asserted low.
109: If a NACK handling timeout occurs or [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`] is cleared, then the FSM will halt again after the STOP condition is sent.
110: The STOP condition terminates the transaction, leaving the FSM halted in the "bus idle" state, with SDA and SCL released.
111: 
112: #### Bus Arbitration
113: 
114: In a multi-controller configuration, the Controller Module may begin transmitting at the same time as another controller.
115: The Bus Monitor will detect when the Controller Module loses arbitration, such as when it attempts to transmit a logic high, but another device is pulling SDA low.
116: The monitor will inform the Controller Module, and the Controller Module will abort its command and halt.
117: The [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.ARBITRATION_LOST`](registers.md#controller_events) bit will be set, and the `controller_halt` interrupt state will reflect that the module is halted.
118: 
119: From here, software must decide what to do.
120: The FMT FIFO will have the entries that remained, but typically, this event will result in software retrying the full transaction.

464: All values are expressed in units of the input clock period.
465: These must be greater than 2 in order for the change in SCL to propagate to the input of the FSM so that acknowledgements are detected correctly.

829: ## HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT
830: Timeout in Host-Mode for an unhandled NACK before hardware automatically ends the transaction.
831: (in units of input clock frequency)
832: 
833: If an active Controller-Transmitter transfer receives a NACK from the Target, the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.NACK`](#controller_events) bit is set.
834: In turn, this causes the Controller FSM to halt awaiting software intervention, and the 'controller_halt' interrupt may assert.
835: Software must clear the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.NACK`](#controller_events) bit to allow the state machine to continue, typically after clearing out the FMTFIFO to start a new transfer.
836: While halted, the active transaction is not ended (no STOP (P) condition is created), and the block asserts SCL and leaves SDA released.
837: 
838: This timeout can be used to automatically produce a STOP condition, whether as a backstop for slow software responses (longer timeout) or as a convenience (short timeout).
839: If the timeout expires, the Controller FSM will issue a STOP (P) condition on the bus to end the active transaction.
840: Additionally, the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.UNHANDLED_NACK_TIMEOUT`](#controller_events) bit is set to alert software, and the FSM will return to the idle state and halt until the bit is cleared.
841: 
842: The enable bit must be set for this feature to operate.
843: - Offset: `0x74`
844: - Reset default: `0x0`
845: - Reset mask: `0xffffffff`
846: 
847: ### Fields
848: 
849: ```wavejson
850: {"reg": [{"name": "VAL", "bits": 31, "attr": ["rw"], "rotate": 0}, {"name": "EN", "bits": 1, "attr": ["rw"], "rotate": -90}], "config": {"lanes": 1, "fontsize": 10, "vspace": 80}}
851: ```
852: 
853: |  Bits  |  Type  |  Reset  | Name   | Description                                                     |
854: |:------:|:------:|:-------:|:-------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
855: |   31   |   rw   |   0x0   | EN     | Timeout enable                                                  |
856: |  30:0  |   rw   |   0x0   | VAL    | Unhandled NAK timeout value (in units of input clock frequency) |
857: 
858: ## CONTROLLER_EVENTS
859: Latched events that explain why the controller halted.
860: 
861: Any bits that are set must be written (with a 1) to clear the CONTROLLER_HALT interrupt.
862: - Offset: `0x78`
863: - Reset default: `0x0`
864: - Reset mask: `0xf`
865: 
866: ### Fields
867: 
868: ```wavejson
869: {"reg": [{"name": "NACK", "bits": 1, "attr": ["rw1c"], "rotate": -90}, {"name": "UNHANDLED_NACK_TIMEOUT", "bits": 1, "attr": ["rw1c"], "rotate": -90}, {"name": "BUS_TIMEOUT", "bits": 1, "attr": ["rw1c"], "rotate": -90}, {"name": "ARBITRATION_LOST", "bits": 1, "attr": ["rw1c"], "rotate": -90}, {"bits": 28}], "config": {"lanes": 1, "fontsize": 10, "vspace": 240}}
870: ```
871: 
872: |  Bits  |  Type  |  Reset  | Name                   | Description                                                                                                               |
873: |:------:|:------:|:-------:|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
874: |  31:4  |        |         |                        | Reserved                                                                                                                  |
875: |   3    |  rw1c  |   0x0   | ARBITRATION_LOST       | A Host-Mode active transaction has terminated due to lost arbitration.                                                    |
876: |   2    |  rw1c  |   0x0   | BUS_TIMEOUT            | A Host-Mode active transaction has terminated due to a bus timeout activated by [`TIMEOUT_CTRL.`](#timeout_ctrl)          |
877: |   1    |  rw1c  |   0x0   | UNHANDLED_NACK_TIMEOUT | A Host-Mode active transaction has been ended by the [`HOST_NACK_HANDLER_TIMEOUT`](#host_nack_handler_timeout) mechanism. |

interface.sampling: Each row action then pre (settled before rising core clock) then post (settled after edge). One row is one executed core cycle. Process previous post -> pre -> post physical SCL/SDA changes. pre ready&valid pops one FMT entry at this edge. Post ready is for next edge.
interface.actions_meaning: rst_n async low reset. enable drives host_enable. push enqueues byte/start/stop/nak_ok in a fixed 64-entry FIFO before pre. Head held until pre ready&valid. flush removes entries before pre (only legal halted/idle context, caller must respect). clear_events clears sticky NACK and timeout before pre. target_ack controls external target ACK at ninth bit; stretch is external open-drain SCL pull-low. nak_timeout_enable/value drive public timeout pins. READB/RCONT fixed zero. No RX expected.
interface.observations_meaning: scl/sda physical wired-AND bus; scl_i/sda_i two-flop synchronized bus; scl_o/sda_o release=1 drive-low=0. ready=fmt_fifo_rready_o, idle=host_idle_o; transmitting=transmitting_o. nak/nak_timeout/arbitration/scl_interference/stretch_timeout/sda_unstable/complete/rx_valid/rx_data corresponding public outputs. valid/depth/fmt_byte/fmt_start/fmt_stop/fmt_nak_ok public FMT inputs. unhandled_nak/unhandled_timeout are sticky event latches. bus_free is independent single-controller free-time monitor. target_low is external SDA pull-down.
interface.environment: Passive write target counts physical SCL rises between START/STOP and ACKs each ninth bit, samples target_ack during low ACK phase; no internal DUT state. It never drives logic high. Stretch only asserted while SCL low (otherwise input assumption violation). No rival controller, sda_interference fixed0. bus_free requires released bus for 6 core cycles after STOP/initial reset; no full bus monitor verification. Event latches set on pre event outputs, cleared by software action. All actions nonnegative two-state integers. Reset clears FIFO, target and sticky events; initial two reset cycles. No model can modify any of these components.
